MUJAHID:v2p769/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v2p769/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v2p769/r1.claim: Mujahid says the fig and olive are the fruits people eat.

FARRA:v3p276/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p276/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
FARRA:v3p276/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the fig and olive as the familiar fruits, or as two Syrian mountains or mosques, one where God spoke to Moses.

FARRA:v3p276/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p276/r2.speaker: رجل من أهل الشام
FARRA:v3p276/r2.claim: A Syrian interpreter says the fig mountains extend from Ḥulwān to Hamadhān and the olive mountains are in Syria.

TAB:95:1/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:95:1/r1.speaker: الحسن
TAB:95:1/r1.claim: Al-Ḥasan takes the oath as the ordinary edible fig and the olive from which oil is pressed.

TAB:95:1/r10.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:95:1/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB:95:1/r10.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the fig is Noah's mosque built on Mount Judi and the olive is Jerusalem; fig, olive, and Sinai are three Syrian mosques.

TAB:95:1/r11.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:95:1/r11.speaker: author
TAB:95:1/r11.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers the ordinary fruits because those are familiar Arabic meanings and no mountains are known by those names; he allows a possible but textually unsupported reference to their growing places.

TAB:95:1/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:95:1/r2.speaker: عكرمة
TAB:95:1/r2.claim: ʿIkrima says the references are the familiar figs and olives people eat.

TAB:95:1/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:95:1/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TAB:95:1/r3.claim: Mujāhid interprets them as the fruit people eat, with olives pressed for oil.

TAB:95:1/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:95:1/r4.speaker: إبراهيم
TAB:95:1/r4.claim: Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī identifies ordinary edible figs and oil-bearing olives.

TAB:95:1/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:95:1/r5.speaker: الكلبي
TAB:95:1/r5.claim: Al-Kalbī says the oath refers to the fig and olive visible to people.

TAB:95:1/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:95:1/r6.speaker: كعب
TAB:95:1/r6.claim: Kaʿb interprets the fig as the mosque of Damascus and the olive as Jerusalem.

TAB:95:1/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:95:1/r7.speaker: قتادة
TAB:95:1/r7.claim: Qatāda reports that the fig and olive are the mountains on which Damascus and Jerusalem stand.

TAB:95:1/r8.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:95:1/r8.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB:95:1/r8.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies the fig as the Damascus mosque and the olive as the mosque of Aelia.

TAB:95:1/r9.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:95:1/r9.speaker: عكرمة
TAB:95:1/r9.claim: A report from ʿIkrima says they are two mountains.

ZAJJAJ:v5p343/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v5p343/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v5p343/r1.claim: Al-tīn and al-zaytūn are variously interpreted as Damascus and Jerusalem; the mountains above those cities; two mountains; or the familiar fig and olive fruits.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447#2/r1.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447#2/r1.claim: Qatadah identifies the fig with the mountain of Damascus and the olive with the mountain of Jerusalem.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447#2/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447#2/r4.speaker: محمد بن كعب
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447#2/r4.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb identifies the fig as the Companions of the Cave's mosque, the olive as Aelia's mosque, Sinai as the Mount's mosque, and the secure city as Mecca.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447#2/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447#2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says the fig and olive are fruits people eat, and Sinai means the Mount, with sinin meaning blessed.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447#2/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447#2/r6.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447#2/r6.claim: Mujahid identifies the fig and olive as edible fruit, Sinai as the blessed Mount, and Mecca as the secure city; he reads best form as finest shape, the lowest state as Hell, and the believers' reward as uncounted.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the fig with Noah's mosque built atop Mount Judi.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3447/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the olive with Jerusalem.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3449#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3449#2/r1.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3449#2/r1.claim: Ikrimah identifies the fig and olive as the fruits themselves, Sinai as the Mount with sinin meaning beauty in Abyssinian, and the secure city as Mecca.

NAHHAS:v5p254/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p254/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p254/r1.claim: The lām assimilates into tāʾ and zāy because they are close; with the definite article it is not pronounced clearly because that construction is frequent.

NAHHAS:v5p254/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p254/r2.speaker: محمد بن كعب
NAHHAS:v5p254/r2.claim: He identifies the fig with the mosque of the Companions of the Cave and the olive with the mosque of Īliyāʾ.

NAHHAS:v5p254/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p254/r3.speaker: قيل
NAHHAS:v5p254/r3.claim: Other views identify the fig with Damascus and the olive with Jerusalem, or take them as two mosques, one where God spoke to Moses.

NAHHAS:v5p254/r4.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p254/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
NAHHAS:v5p254/r4.claim: As transmitted by ʿIkrima, he identifies them as the actual figs and olives people know.

NAHHAS:v5p254/r5.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p254/r5.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p254/r5.claim: These interpretations converge on the implied oath ‘by the Lord of the fig and olive.’

SULAMI:v2p406/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p406/r1.speaker: الجنيد
SULAMI:v2p406/r1.claim: The fig and olive signify Jerusalem's mosque, Sinai signifies its mosque, and the secure city signifies Mecca's mosque; God swore by these places because He is remembered there, and any place of remembrance is exalted.

THALABI:v10p238#3/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p238#3/r1.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وعكرمة وإبراهيم وعطاء بن أبي رباح وجابر بن زيد ومقاتل والكلبي
THALABI:v10p238#3/r1.claim: They identify the fig and olive as the familiar fruits people eat and press for oil.

THALABI:v10p238#3/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p238#3/r2.speaker: النبي
THALABI:v10p238#3/r2.claim: After eating a gift of figs, the Prophet said that if any fruit had descended from Paradise it would be this; he said it has no pits and benefits hemorrhoids and gout.

THALABI:v10p238#3/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p238#3/r3.speaker: النبي
THALABI:v10p238#3/r3.claim: The Prophet praised olive wood as a good siwak, said it sweetens the mouth, and called it his and earlier prophets’ tooth-stick from the blessed tree.

THALABI:v10p238#3/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p238#3/r4.speaker: كعب الأحبار وقتادة وابن زيد وعبد الرحمن بن غنيم
THALABI:v10p238#3/r4.claim: They interpret the fig as Damascus Mosque and the olive as Jerusalem.

THALABI:v10p238#3/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p238#3/r5.speaker: الضحاك
THALABI:v10p238#3/r5.claim: He says the fig and olive signify two mosques in Syria.

THALABI:v10p238#3/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p238#3/r6.speaker: محمد بن كعب
THALABI:v10p238#3/r6.claim: He identifies the fig as the Companions of the Cave’s mosque and the olive as the mosque of Ilya, taking the names to mean their growing places.

THALABI:v10p238#3/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p238#3/r7.speaker: عكرمة
THALABI:v10p238#3/r7.claim: He says the fig and olive are two mountains.

THALABI:v10p238#3/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p238#3/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v10p238#3/r8.claim: Through Atiyya, he identifies the fig with Noah’s mosque built on al-Judi and the olive with Jerusalem.

THALABI:v10p238#3/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p238#3/r9.speaker: الضحاك
THALABI:v10p238#3/r9.claim: Through Nahshal, he identifies the fig as the Sacred Mosque and the olive as al-Aqsa.

THALABI:v10p239/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p239/r1.speaker: رجل من أهل الشام
THALABI:v10p239/r1.claim: A Syrian commentator told al-Farra that the fig mountains run from Helwan to Hamadan and the olive mountains are in Syria.

THALABI:v10p239/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p239/r10.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
THALABI:v10p239/r10.claim: He lists four sacred mountains: Damascus, Jerusalem, Moses’ mountain, and Mecca, respectively called Tur Tinna, Tur Zayta, Tur Sina, and Tur Yatmana.

THALABI:v10p239/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p239/r11.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
THALABI:v10p239/r11.claim: He recited the verse at Mecca with the reading ‘Tur Sina’; the narrator thought he did so to teach the city’s sanctity.

THALABI:v10p239/r18.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p239/r18.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p239/r18.claim: The continuation identifies the olive as the Mosque of al-Aqsa.

THALABI:v10p239/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p239/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p239/r2.claim: Mount Sinai means the mountain of Moses.

THALABI:v10p239/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p239/r9.speaker: شهر بن حوشب
THALABI:v10p239/r9.claim: He identifies the fig as Kufa, the olive as Syria, and Mount Sinin as a mountain bearing many kinds of trees.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r1.claim: Mawardi reports a Makkan dating from al-Hasan, Ikrima, Ata, and Jabir, while Ibn Abbas and Qatada say the sura is Medinan.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r2.speaker: الحسن، عكرمة، مجاهد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r2.claim: These authorities identify the fig and olive as the edible fruits.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r3.speaker: كعب الأحبار، ابن زيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r3.claim: Ka'b al-Ahbar and Ibn Zayd interpret the fig as Damascus and the olive as Jerusalem.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r4.speaker: الحارث، ابن زيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r4.claim: Al-Harith and Ibn Zayd identify them as the mosque of Damascus and the mosque of Jerusalem.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r5.speaker: ابن قتيبة، الربيع
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r5.claim: Ibn Qutayba and al-Rabi' identify two Syrian mountains, called Mount Zayta and Mount Tina; Ibn al-Anbari's alternative location between Hulwan and Hamadan is called far-fetched by Mawardi.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r6.speaker: محمد بن كعب
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r6.claim: Muhammad ibn Ka'b says the fig is the mosque of the Companions of the Cave and the olive the mosque of Iliya.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas says the fig is Noah's mosque on al-Judi and the olive is Jerusalem's mosque.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r8.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p300/r8.claim: Mawardi allows that the fruits stand for God's blessings, since figs are food and olives a condiment.

QUSHAYRI:v3p434/r1.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p434/r1.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p434/r1.claim: God's name signals His eternal majesty and beauty, and points to His eternal reception and generosity.

QUSHAYRI:v3p434/r2.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p434/r2.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p434/r2.claim: The knower is overwhelmed by divine majesty, the chosen one lives through divine beauty, the saint trembles at divine acceptance, and the seeker needs no livelihood alongside God's sufficiency.

QUSHAYRI:v3p434/r3.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p434/r3.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p434/r3.claim: The fig is a great blessing because it has no pit, is free of irritating blemish, and is sized to complete the pleasure of a single bite.

QUSHAYRI:v3p434/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p434/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p434/r4.claim: The olive has many uses, including providing lamp oil, food seasoning, and a dipping condiment.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس عن الكلبي والحسن ومجاهد وعكرمة وإبراهيم ومقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r1.claim: They identify the fig and olive as the familiar fruits that people eat and press for oil.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r2.claim: The fig is a pure fruit whose concentrated pleasure and careful preparation point to its Creator and invite gratitude.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r3.speaker: أبو ذر عن النبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r3.claim: A report says the fig came from Paradise, has no seeds, and should be eaten because it helps hemorrhoids and gout; the source states no grading.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r4.claim: Olives yield oil used in foods, dressings, and soap; their trees provide lasting wealth, fragrance, and nourishment when eaten before pressing.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r5.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r5.claim: He identifies the fig as the mountain of Damascus and the olive as the mountain of Jerusalem.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r6.speaker: ابن زيد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r6.claim: He gives the same places but specifies the mosques of Damascus and Jerusalem.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r7.speaker: عكرمة عن أبي مكين
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r7.claim: He says the fig and olive are two mountains.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r8.speaker: الفراء عن رجل صاحب تفسير
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r8.claim: He reports that fig names mountains between Hulwan and Hamadhan, while olive names the mountains of Syria; those places take their names from the plants growing there.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p143#2/r9.claim: On the place-name interpretation, the phrase can omit a noun and mean the places where figs and olives grow.

WAHIDI-QT:95:1/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:95:1/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:95:1/r1.claim: Al-tin and al-zaytun are two mountains in Syria, Mount Tina and Mount Zayta in Syriac, named for the trees that grow there.

JISHUMI:v10p7469/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r1.speaker: أبي بن كعب
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r1.claim: A report from the Prophet promises health and certainty during life and a reward after death equal to a day's fasting multiplied by the chapter's reciters.

JISHUMI:v10p7469/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r10.claim: He also explains the fig as Noah's mosque and the olive as Jerusalem.

JISHUMI:v10p7469/r11.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r11.speaker: الضحاك
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r11.claim: He explains the two fruits as two mosques in Syria.

JISHUMI:v10p7469/r12.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r12.speaker: محمد بن كعب
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r12.claim: He identifies the fig as the mosque of the People of the Cave and the olive as the mosque of Iliya.

JISHUMI:v10p7469/r13.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r13.speaker: الأصم
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r13.claim: He says the fig and olive are named with Mount Sinai because they grow on that mountain and display God's power through their contrasting qualities.

JISHUMI:v10p7469/r14.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r14.speaker: عكرمة
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r14.claim: He says the fig and olive are two mountains.

JISHUMI:v10p7469/r15.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r15.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r15.claim: Other reported explanations identify them as Kufa and Syria, the places where prophets arose, or the Sacred Mosque and the Aqsa Mosque.

JISHUMI:v10p7469/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r2.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r2.claim: After al-Sharḥ commands desire for God, this chapter says God created and transformed creation; therefore worship and needs should be directed to Him alone.

JISHUMI:v10p7469/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r8.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r8.claim: God may swear by the fig and olive themselves or by their Lord; they are singled out for benefits and as signs of creative power, since fig grows from wood and olive yields oil.

JISHUMI:v10p7469/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r9.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وعطاء بن أبي رباح وقتادة وعكرمة وإبراهيم وجابر بن زيد ومقاتل والكلبي وأبو علي وأبو مسلم
JISHUMI:v10p7469/r9.claim: They identify the fig as the fruit and the olive as the fruit pressed for oil; the author prefers this apparent sense absent evidence to leave it.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وإبراهيم وعطاء بن أبي رباح ومقاتل والكلبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r1.claim: These authorities identify the fig and olive as the familiar fruits people eat and press for oil.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r2.claim: The fig is singled out because it is a pure fruit without seeds and resembles the fruits of Paradise.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r3.claim: The olive is singled out for its many benefits and as a blessed tree mentioned in a report; its fruit and oil serve for food and lighting.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r4.speaker: عكرمة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r4.claim: Ikrima interprets the fig and olive as two mountains.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r5.speaker: قتادة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r5.claim: Qatada identifies the fig mountain as the one bearing Damascus and the olive mountain as the one bearing Jerusalem, named for the trees growing there.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r6.speaker: الضحاك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r6.claim: Al-Dahhak interprets the two words as two mosques in Syria.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r7.speaker: ابن زيد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r7.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies the fig as the Mosque of Damascus and the olive as the Mosque of Jerusalem.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r8.speaker: محمد بن كعب
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p468#2/r8.claim: Muhammad ibn Kab identifies the fig as the mosque of the People of the Cave and the olive as the Mosque of Iliya.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r1.claim: Figs and olives are wondrous among fruit-bearing trees; reports mention their virtues and use as food and tooth-stick.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r10.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r10.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r10.claim: The oath honors blessed places through the good associated with prophets and righteous people: Abraham migrated to the fig-and-olive region, Jesus was born and raised there, Moses was called at the Mount, and Muhammad was born and sent in Mecca.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r2.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r2.claim: A report says the Prophet ate a plate of figs, called them a fruit of Paradise if any could be so called, and described them as seedless and beneficial for hemorrhoids and gout.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r3.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r3.claim: Muadh passed an olive tree, took a branch for brushing his teeth, and said he heard the Prophet praise olive wood as a blessed tooth-stick that freshens the mouth and helps the teeth.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r4.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r4.claim: The Prophet is also reported to say that olive wood was his tooth-stick and that of earlier prophets.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets the words as referring to your Prophet and your olives.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r6.claim: Alternatively, the words name two mountains in the Holy Land, called in Syriac Tur Tina and Tur Zayta because figs and olives grow there.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r7.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p778/r7.claim: Another view places the fig mountains between Hulwan and Hamadan, and the olive mountains in Syria, identifying their growing regions.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p780/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p780/r2.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p780/r2.claim: A report promises health and certainty in this life to whoever recites Surat al-Tin, and after death a reward equal to the number of its reciters.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وعكرمة وإبراهيم وعطاء وجابر بن زيد ومقاتل
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r1.claim: These authorities identify the oath's fig and olive as the familiar fruit and oil-producing tree.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r2.claim: A report says the Prophet ate gifted figs and praised them as a fruit from Paradise, without pits and useful for hemorrhoids and gout.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r3.claim: A report calls olive-wood tooth sticks excellent and says prophets before Muhammad used them.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r4.speaker: كعب وعكرمة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r4.claim: Kaʿb and Ikrima take the oath as referring to the regions where figs grow at Damascus and olives at Iliya.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r5.speaker: قتادة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r5.claim: Qatada identifies two Levantine mountains, one bearing Damascus and the other Jerusalem.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r6.speaker: ابن زيد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r6.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies the fig with the Damascus mosque and the olive with the mosque of Iliya.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r7.claim: Another interpretation identifies them as Noah's mosque and Abraham's mosque.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r9.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p499#2/r9.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi says the fig is the People of the Cave mosque and the olive the mosque of Iliya.

TABRISI:95:1-3/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:95:1-3/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:95:1-3/r2.claim: The oath refers literally to the edible fig and the olive from which oil is pressed; al-Hasan, Mujahid, ʿIkrima, and Qatada agree.

TABRISI:95:1-3/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:95:1-3/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:95:1-3/r3.claim: Al-Tabrisi prefers the literal fruit reading as the apparent meaning; the fig's size, smoothness, and design show divine favor.

TABRISI:95:1-3/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:95:1-3/r4.speaker: أبو ذر
TABRISI:95:1-3/r4.claim: A report from Abu Dharr quotes the Prophet praising the fig as a fruit from Paradise, without pits, and as beneficial for hemorrhoids and breath.

TABRISI:95:1-3/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:95:1-3/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:95:1-3/r5.claim: Olive oil is used as a condiment in many foods, and the fig is a nourishing food with many benefits.

TABRISI:95:1-3/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:95:1-3/r6.speaker: قتادة
TABRISI:95:1-3/r6.claim: One geographical interpretation takes the fig and olive as mountains associated with Damascus and Jerusalem.

TABRISI:95:1-3/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:95:1-3/r7.speaker: كعب الأحبار
TABRISI:95:1-3/r7.claim: The fig may mean the mosque of Damascus and the olive the Temple in Jerusalem; ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm and Ibn Zayd share this view.

TABRISI:95:1-3/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:95:1-3/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:95:1-3/r8.claim: Another interpretation identifies the fig with Noah's mosque on Mount Judi and the olive with Jerusalem.

TABRISI:95:1-3/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:95:1-3/r9.speaker: الضحاك
TABRISI:95:1-3/r9.claim: Al-Dahhak identifies the fig with the Sacred Mosque in Mecca and the olive with al-Aqsa.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r1.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن وعطاء ومجاهد وعكرمة وجابر بن زيد وإبراهيم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r1.claim: The oath can refer to the familiar fig and familiar olive; some interpreters add that the fig's pure, unspoiled fruit and the olive's many uses display God's power.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r2.speaker: ابن عباس عن عطية
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r2.claim: The fig is Noah's mosque built on al-Jūdī, and the olive is Jerusalem.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r3.speaker: الضحاك
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r3.claim: The fig is the Sacred Mosque in Mecca and the olive is al-Aqṣā Mosque.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r4.speaker: كعب وقتادة وابن زيد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r4.claim: The fig is the mosque of Damascus and the olive is Jerusalem.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r5.speaker: عكرمة وقتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r5.claim: They may be two mountains: the mountain of Damascus and the mountain of Jerusalem.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r6.speaker: القرظي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r6.claim: The fig is the mosque of the People of the Cave and the olive is the mosque of Īliyāʾ.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r7.speaker: الفراء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p168/r7.claim: The fig means mountains from Ḥulwān to Hamadhān, and the olive means mountains in Syria.

RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r1.claim: The fig and olive may name two mountains in the Holy Land; their regions evoke prophetic origins, with Jesus, Israelite prophets, Moses, and Muhammad associated with the sites in sequence.

RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r2.claim: A second view takes the names as mosques: Ibn Zayd identifies them as the Damascus mosque and the Jerusalem mosque.

RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r3.speaker: آخرون
RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r3.claim: Other mosque identifications are the mosque of the Cave Companions and Ilya; Ibn ʿAbbas instead names Noah's mosque on al-Judi and the Jerusalem mosque.

RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r4.claim: Those who read the terms as mosques prefer swearing by worship places, and say the place names stand for regions rich in figs and olives.

RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r5.speaker: كعب
RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r5.claim: A third view takes fig as Damascus and olive as Jerusalem; Shahr ibn Hawshab instead identifies Kufa and Syria, while al-Rabiʿ names mountains between Hamadan and Hulwan.

RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p10/r6.claim: The country readings may honor lands revered by Jews, Christians, Muslims, and Quraysh, or distinguish Damascus and Jerusalem's worldly blessings from Sinai and Mecca's religious blessings.

RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r1.claim: Unlike fruits whose outer and inner parts differ in quality, the fig is good both outside and inside.

RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r2.claim: The fig bears fruit before showing flowers or leaves; unlike other trees, it gives before displaying itself, an image of generosity that al-Razi compares to the Prophet's selflessness and the Anṣar.

RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r3.claim: A saying compares other trees to the instruction to begin with oneself and dependents, while the fig tree resembles the Chosen Prophet, who begins with others.

RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r4.claim: Unlike other trees, a fig tree can produce another crop after its fruit falls in the same year.

RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r5.claim: In dream interpretation, a fig signifies a good, wealthy man; receiving it predicts wealth and abundance, while eating it predicts children.

RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r6.claim: Reports say Adam covered himself with fig leaves after disobedience; a second tale says the first gazelles he fed gained beauty and musk, while later greedy ones gained only beauty.

RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r7.claim: The olive tree is blessed: it serves as fruit, condiment, and medicine, needs little cultivation, and produces oil for both food and lamps.

RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r8.claim: Dreaming of an olive leaf signifies holding firmly to the strongest handhold; Ibn Sirin advises a sick dreamer to eat olives after interpreting a cryptic vision.

RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p9#2/r9.claim: Al-Razi prefers the literal fruits, concluding that their great benefits are the reason God swears by them.

RAZI-FULL:v32p9/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p9/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p9/r1.claim: To explain why God swears by apparently ordinary fruits, one view takes fig and olive literally; Ibn ʿAbbas says they are the familiar local fruits.

RAZI-FULL:v32p9/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p9/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v32p9/r2.claim: The fig is described as food, fruit, and medicine; physicians attribute digestive, laxative, and other bodily benefits to it.

RAZI-FULL:v32p9/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p9/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
RAZI-FULL:v32p9/r3.claim: A report says a plate of figs was brought to the Prophet, who called them a fruit from Paradise, seedless, and beneficial for hemorrhoids and gout.

RAZI-FULL:v32p9/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v32p9/r4.speaker: علي بن موسى الرضا
RAZI-FULL:v32p9/r4.claim: ʿAli al-Rida says figs freshen the mouth, lengthen hair, protect against paralysis, and can be used to expel bodily excess.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r1.claim: The fig recalls the leaves Adam used to cover himself in Paradise.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r10.claim: Qurtubi's preferred ruling requires zakat on both figs and olives, while urging people to give God His due.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r2.claim: Another explanation says the fig is sworn by to display its great blessing: attractive, fragrant, delicious, easy to pick, and small enough for a bite.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r3.speaker: الشاعر
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r3.claim: One poem likens the fig's split skin and bowed neck to a once-rich person stripped of new clothing.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r4.speaker: الشاعر
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r4.claim: A second poem praises the sweet fig hanging from its branch, with a face like one bowing in awe of God.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r5.claim: The olive recalls Abraham's image of a blessed olive tree.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r6.claim: Olive is a staple in Syria and the Maghreb, used as relish, in cooking, as lamp oil, and for internal ailments, sores, and wounds.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r7.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r7.claim: A prophetic report recommends eating and applying olive oil because it comes from a blessed tree.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r8.speaker: ابن العربي
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r8.claim: Ibn al-Arabi argues that because figs are a divine bounty and a stored staple, their zakat should be paid; rulers' unjust collection made many scholars avoid stating this.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r9.speaker: الشافعي
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1#2/r9.claim: Al-Shafi'i says olives are not subject to zakat, partly for the same concern about rulers' exactions.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r1.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وعكرمة وإبراهيم النخعي وعطاء بن أبي رباح وجابر بن زيد ومقاتل والكلبي
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r1.claim: These authorities identify the oath's fig and olive as the familiar edible fig and oil-bearing olive, with the olive tree also described in the Qur'an.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r10.speaker: الفراء
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r10.claim: Al-Farra quotes a Syrian informant who places the fig in mountains between Hulwan and Hamadan and the olive in the Syrian mountains.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r11.claim: Another view says the names are two Syrian mountains called Tur Zayta and Tur Tina in Syriac because they grow olives and figs; Abu Makin transmits the mountain view from Ikrima.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r12.speaker: النابغة
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r12.claim: Al-Nabigha's poetry uses al-Tin as a place name, supporting a geographical reading.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r13.speaker: النحاس
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r13.claim: Al-Nahhas allows an omitted possessive, meaning the places where figs and olives grow, but says neither the Qur'an's surface nor an authoritative report supports it.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r14.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r14.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r14.claim: Qurtubi considers the ordinary fruits the soundest interpretation because it is literal and one should not leave literal meaning for metaphor without evidence.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r2.speaker: أبو ذر
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r2.claim: Abu Dharr reports a tray of figs given to the Prophet; he ate them and said that, if any fruit came from Paradise, it would be this seedless fruit, which helps hemorrhoids and gout.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r3.speaker: معاذ
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r3.claim: Muadh reports using an olive twig as a toothstick and hearing the Prophet praise olive as blessed, freshening the mouth and removing dental decay.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas also identifies the fig with Noah's mosque built on Judi and the olive with the Jerusalem mosque.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r5.speaker: الضحاك
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r5.claim: Al-Dahhak says the fig is the Sacred Mosque and the olive is al-Aqsa Mosque.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r6.speaker: ابن زيد
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r6.claim: Ibn Zayd gives two geographical readings: Damascus Mosque with Jerusalem Mosque, or Damascus with Jerusalem.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r7.speaker: قتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r7.claim: Qatada identifies the two fruits with the mountains above Damascus and Jerusalem respectively.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r8.speaker: محمد بن كعب
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r8.claim: Muhammad ibn Ka'b says the fig is the Cave Companions' mosque and the olive is the mosque of Iliya.

QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r9.speaker: كعب الأحبار وقتادة وعكرمة وابن زيد
QURTUBI-FULL:95:1/r9.claim: Ka'b al-Ahbar, Qatada, Ikrima, and Ibn Zayd identify the fig with Damascus and the olive with Jerusalem; al-Tabari chooses this interpretation.

BAYDAWI-FULL:95:1-2/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:95:1-2/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:95:1-2/r1.claim: Figs and olives are singled out for their pleasant, seasonless, easily digested food and many medicinal benefits; a report adds hemorrhoid and gout treatment.

BAYDAWI-FULL:95:1-2/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:95:1-2/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:95:1-2/r2.claim: A Prophetic report says figs cut hemorrhoids and benefit gout; no grading is stated.

BAYDAWI-FULL:95:1-2/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:95:1-2/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:95:1-2/r3.claim: The two names may instead indicate mountains of the Holy Land, the mosques of Damascus and Jerusalem, or the regions themselves.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r1.claim: The fig and olive are singled out in the oath as remarkable among fruit-bearing trees.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r2.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r2.claim: When given a plate of figs, the Prophet ate them and invited his companions to eat, saying that if any fruit came from Paradise it would be this one, since Paradise fruit has no seeds; he said figs cure hemorrhoids and gout.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r3.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r3.claim: The Prophet praised olive wood as a blessed-tree toothstick that freshens the mouth and removes tooth decay, and said it was his toothstick and that of earlier prophets.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the fig and olive as the familiar local fruits.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r5.speaker: قيل
NASAFI-FULL:v4p347#2/r5.claim: Another interpretation identifies them as two mountains in Syria where figs and olives grow.

QASHANI:95:1-3/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:95:1-3/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:95:1-3/r1.claim: The fig is universal meaning abstracted from particulars and perceived by the heart: immaterial, precise, strengthening, and pleasurable, like fruit that is all pulp and contains seeds within it.

QASHANI:95:1-3/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:95:1-3/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:95:1-3/r4.claim: These oaths honor the means of human existence and perfection: universal and particular meanings, heart and self, perceivers and what they perceive.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r1.claim: Al-tīn can mean the familiar fruit or a mountain, with exegetical views to follow.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r2.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r2.claim: The surah is Meccan for most commentators; Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatada say Madinan.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r3.claim: After praising the Prophet's perfected creation and character, the surah describes the one who opposes him being brought low in this world and the next; mankind was created ready to accept truth but may be moved to a base state.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r4.claim: The apparent meaning of the fig and olive is the well-known fruit, though the commentary next records place-based interpretations.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r5.claim: A report praises figs as useful for hemorrhoids and gout.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r6.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وعكرمة والنخعي وعطاء بن أبي رباح وجابر بن زيد ومقاتل والكلبي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r6.claim: These authorities identify the olive with the blessed tree emerging from Mount Sinai.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r7.speaker: كعب وعكرمة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r7.claim: Kaʿb and ʿIkrima say the oath is by the regions where figs and olives grow: Damascus and Īliyāʾ.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r8.speaker: قتادة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r8.claim: Qatada identifies the fig and olive as two Syrian mountains, one bearing Damascus and the other Jerusalem.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p502/r9.claim: Other interpreters identify them as two mosques, but their proposed locations vary widely; the author sets that debate aside.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p503/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p503/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p503/r6.claim: The oath highlights the honor and good associated with these places through prophets and righteous people: Abraham and Jesus in the fig-and-olive region, Moses at the Mount, and Muhammad's birthplace, mission, and sanctuary at Mecca.

IBNKATHIR:95:1/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:95:1/r2.speaker: البراء بن عازب
IBNKATHIR:95:1/r2.claim: A report transmitted in the collections says the Prophet recited al-Tīn in one of two travel prayers; al-Barāʾ had never heard anyone with better voice or recitation.

IBNKATHIR:95:1/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:95:1/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:95:1/r3.claim: The fig is said to be Damascus's mosque, the fig itself, or the mountain beside Damascus.

IBNKATHIR:95:1/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:95:1/r4.speaker: القرطبي
IBNKATHIR:95:1/r4.claim: Al-Qurṭubī says the fig is the mosque of the People of the Cave.

IBNKATHIR:95:1/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:95:1/r5.speaker: ابن عباس عن العوفي
IBNKATHIR:95:1/r5.claim: The fig is Noah's mosque on al-Jūdī.

IBNKATHIR:95:1/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:95:1/r6.speaker: مجاهد
IBNKATHIR:95:1/r6.claim: The fig means the actual fig fruit.

IBNKATHIR:95:1/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:95:1/r7.speaker: كعب الأحبار وقتادة وابن زيد
IBNKATHIR:95:1/r7.claim: The olive is the mosque in Jerusalem.

IBNKATHIR:95:1/r8.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:95:1/r8.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة
IBNKATHIR:95:1/r8.claim: The olive is the actual olive that people press.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#s095/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#s095/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#s095/r1.claim: The surah’s purpose is to establish God’s complete power: the wonders of fig and olive creation, prophethood, and the human being—the cosmos’s most marvelous creature—support it.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#s095/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#s095/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468#s095/r2.claim: Its oaths point to the honor and marvels of the objects sworn by and of lands blessed by prophets and righteous people.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p468/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468/r1.claim: The surah’s purpose is to establish God’s complete power: the wonders of fig and olive creation, prophethood, and the human being—the cosmos’s most marvelous creature—support it.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p468/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p468/r2.claim: The oath signals the honor of these things and the sacred lands associated with prophets, whose histories and blessings display divine power.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r1.claim: The fig combines pleasure with broad dietary and medicinal benefits, making it unusually complete among fruits.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r2.claim: Though excellent when fresh or dried, the fig spoils quickly and becomes useless; its rise and decline resemble human nature's original openness and later corruption.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r3.claim: The fig's first state is easy, beautiful, and receptive to improvement or change, like the human being's original disposition.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r4.claim: The fig is named first because it receives the greater emphasis in the oath.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r5.claim: The olive is durable and useful as food, medicine, oil, and ointment; it follows the fig as an emblem of the believer.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r6.claim: The trees allude to the Holy Land and Syria, evoking the prophets who lived there, especially Abraham and his descendants.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p470/r7.claim: Using the two trees to signify their lands and inhabitants is more eloquent than naming the people directly.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p475/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p475/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p475/r5.claim: The surah's oath recalls the Torah's account of God coming from Sinai, Seir, and Paran; ideal creation, the righteous, and the fallen summarize the Torah's beginnings, laws, and later history.

DURR-FULL:v8p553/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r1.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r1.claim: The surah is Meccan and has eight verses.

DURR-FULL:v8p553/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r2.claim: He said the surah was revealed in Mecca.

DURR-FULL:v8p553/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r3.claim: He likewise said the surah was revealed in Mecca.

DURR-FULL:v8p553/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r4.speaker: البراء بن عازب
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r4.claim: While traveling, the Prophet recited the Fig and Olive surah in one rakʿah of the night prayer; al-Baraʾ praised his voice and recitation.

DURR-FULL:v8p553/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r5.speaker: عبد الله بن يزيد
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r5.claim: He said the Prophet recited this surah in the sunset prayer.

DURR-FULL:v8p553/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r6.speaker: البراء بن عازب
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r6.claim: He said the Prophet recited this surah in the sunset prayer.

DURR-FULL:v8p553/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r7.speaker: زرعة بن خليفة
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r7.claim: After accepting Islam, he heard the Prophet recite this surah and the Decree surah in the dawn prayer.

DURR-FULL:v8p553/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r8.claim: An explicitly weak report identifies the Fig with Syria and Olive with Palestine, Sinai with Moses' mountain, and the secure town with Mecca; it allegorizes the human as Muhammad, the lowest as idolaters, and the exception as the four caliphs.

DURR-FULL:v8p553/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p553/r9.claim: He identified the Fig as Noah's mosque on al-Judi, Olive as Jerusalem, Sinai as its mosque, and the secure town as Mecca; return to the lowest means extreme old age, excusing contemporaries whose minds failed and preserving their prior reward.

DURR-FULL:v8p554/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p554/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p554/r1.claim: He identified Fig and Olive as the Sacred Mosque and al-Aqsa, where the Night Journey ended; Sinai as Moses' mountain, Mecca as the secure town, upright stature as standing erect, and the lowest as decrepit age.

DURR-FULL:v8p554/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p554/r2.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v8p554/r2.claim: He identified the Fig with Damascus's mountain and Olive with Jerusalem's, Sinai as a blessed wooded mountain and Mecca as the secure town; the oath ends at verse 4, the lowest is Hell, and the final command means be certain of God's proof.

DURR-FULL:v8p554/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p554/r3.speaker: أبو عبد الله الفارسي
DURR-FULL:v8p554/r3.claim: He identified the Fig with Damascus's mosque, the Olive with Jerusalem, Sinai with Moses' mountain, and the secure town with the Sacred City.

DURR-FULL:v8p554/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p554/r4.speaker: محمد بن كعب
DURR-FULL:v8p554/r4.claim: He identified the Fig as the Companions of the Cave's mosque, the Olive as Elijah's mosque, Sinai as the Mount's mosque, and the secure town as Mecca.

DURR-FULL:v8p554/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p554/r5.speaker: الضحاك
DURR-FULL:v8p554/r5.claim: He said the Fig and Olive are two mosques in Syria; Sinai is the mountain, and Sinīn means beautiful.

DURR-FULL:v8p554/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p554/r6.speaker: كعب الأحبار
DURR-FULL:v8p554/r6.claim: He identified the Fig as Damascus, the Olive as Jerusalem, Sinai as where God spoke to Moses, and the secure town as Mecca.

DURR-FULL:v8p554/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p554/r7.speaker: أبو حبيب الحارث بن محمد
DURR-FULL:v8p554/r7.claim: He named four sacred mountains: Zayta/Jerusalem, Sinai, Tina/Damascus, and Tima/Mecca, linking them to the four oaths.

DURR-FULL:v8p555/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p555/r1.speaker: زيد بن ميسرة
DURR-FULL:v8p555/r1.claim: He repeated the sacred-mountain identification and specified Sinai as where God spoke to Moses.

DURR-FULL:v8p555/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p555/r2.speaker: الحكم
DURR-FULL:v8p555/r2.claim: He identified the Fig with Damascus, Olive with Palestine, and the secure town with Mecca.

DURR-FULL:v8p555/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p555/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p555/r3.claim: He identified the Fig and Olive as fruits people eat, and glossed Sinai as the blessed mountain.

DURR-FULL:v8p555/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p555/r4.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v8p555/r4.claim: He identified the first oaths as fruit, the blessed mountain, and Mecca; human creation is in the finest image, return is to Fire, believers are excepted, and their reward is uncounted.

DURR-FULL:v8p555/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p555/r7.speaker: الربيع
DURR-FULL:v8p555/r7.claim: He identified the oath as the mountain bearing fig and olive trees.

DURR-FULL:v8p555/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p555/r9.speaker: عمرو بن ميمون
DURR-FULL:v8p555/r9.claim: He recited with ʿUmar the variant طور سينا, also reported as ʿAbd Allah's reading; ʿUmar paired al-Fil and Quraysh in the next rakʿah and raised his voice to honor the sanctuary.

DURR-FULL:v8p556/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p556/r3.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v8p556/r3.claim: He identified the oaths with actual figs and olives, Sinai as the blessed mountain, and Mecca; finest form is youth and strength, senility is the lowest, and the believer retains reward without reproach.

DURR-FULL:v8p556/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p556/r4.speaker: الحسن
DURR-FULL:v8p556/r4.claim: He identified the oaths with actual figs and olives, finest form with a beautiful image, and the lowest with Hell.

BURSEVI:v10p359/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p359/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p359/r1.claim: The oaths name the edible fig and the olive from which oil is pressed, singled out from other fruits for their notable qualities.

BURSEVI:v10p359/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p359/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p359/r2.claim: The fig is sweet, light, and quickly digested; the source lists many medicinal benefits, including loosening the bowels, dissolving phlegm, cleansing the kidneys, removing bladder gravel, and aiding the body.

BURSEVI:v10p359/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p359/r3.speaker: أبو ذر
BURSEVI:v10p359/r3.claim: Abu Dharr reports that the Prophet ate a gift of figs and urged the companions to eat them, saying that if a fruit descended from Paradise it would be this seedless fruit; he also attributed relief for hemorrhoids and gout to it.

BURSEVI:v10p359/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p359/r4.speaker: علي بن موسى الرضى
BURSEVI:v10p359/r4.claim: ‘Ali ibn Musa al-Rida says figs freshen the breath, lengthen hair, and protect from paralysis.

BURSEVI:v10p359/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p359/r5.speaker: الإمام
BURSEVI:v10p359/r5.claim: A report says Adam covered himself with fig leaves after sin; when lonely after descending, he fed leaves to visiting gazelles, and God made the first group beautiful and gave them musk because they came for Adam rather than for food; later, greedy gazelles gained beauty without musk.

BURSEVI:v10p359/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p359/r6.speaker: أسئلة الحكم
BURSEVI:v10p359/r6.claim: A cited wisdom text says the fig first appears without a covering because it alone covered Adam: after it covered him, God made it bring forth meaning before claim, while other trees show claim before meaning.

BURSEVI:v10p359/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p359/r7.speaker: خريدة العجائب
BURSEVI:v10p359/r7.claim: Khuraydat al-‘Aja’ib says fig-wood ash kills garden worms and its smoke drives away flies and mosquitoes.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r1.claim: The oath concerns blessed, honored places: Makkah is certainly the secure city, home of the House, the Prophet's birth, and his mission.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r14.speaker: قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r14.claim: He identifies the fig mountain with Damascus and the olive mountain with Jerusalem.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r15.speaker: أبو حبيب الحارث بن محمد
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r15.claim: He says the names refer to the two places' fig and olive growth, by ellipsis or figurative naming of the source regions.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r16.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r16.speaker: أبو عبد الله الفارسي
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r16.claim: He identifies the fig with Damascus Mosque and the olive with Jerusalem's holy site, likely because each has a tree of that kind.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r17.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r17.speaker: كعب الأحبار
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r17.claim: He takes the two names as Damascus and Aelia, Jerusalem, using the place-name for its inhabitants.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r18.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r18.speaker: محمد بن كعب
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r18.claim: He identifies them as the Mosque of the Companions of the Cave and the Mosque of Aelia.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r19.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r19.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r19.claim: He identifies the fig and olive with Noah's mosque built on al-Jūdī and Jerusalem.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r20.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r20.speaker: شهر بن حوشب
ALUSI-FULL:v30p173#2/r20.claim: He identifies them as Kufa and Syria; the author notes Kufa was founded in the Islamic period and suggests he may mean its older region.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r1.claim: Some say Kufa existed earlier but was rebuilt under ʿUmar; others identify the locations as mountains between Ḥulwān and Hamadān and the Syrian mountains where these trees grew.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r10.claim: The author favors the sacred-place interpretation: the named trees or their fruits signify the blessings of the holy land, Moses' mountain, and secure Makkah.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r11.speaker: الكشف
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r11.claim: It says the fruits signify earthly and religious blessings of the holy land, while the mountain and secure city complete the image of a blessed land and its greatest protection.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r2.claim: Whatever the referents, the paired terms correspond as particular places, preserving the geographic pattern of the oath.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r3.claim: He also interprets the words as the familiar fruits people eat; al-Ḥākim authenticates this report.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r4.speaker: مجاهد، إبراهيم النخعي، عطاء بن أبي رباح، جابر بن زيد، مقاتل، الكلبي، عكرمة، الحسن
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r4.claim: They are also reported to identify the fruits as ordinary figs and olives.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r5.claim: On the fruit reading, God singles out these fruits for their notable nutritional and medicinal qualities; the author lists benefits attributed to figs.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r6.speaker: أبو ذر
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r6.claim: A report says the Prophet ate gifted figs and praised them as a heavenly fruit that helps hemorrhoids and gout; the author cannot find it in hadith sources.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r7.speaker: داود الطبيب
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r7.claim: The physician Dawud calls a hadith on figs helping hemorrhoids sound, and discusses their benefits with particular preparations.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r8.claim: Olives are described as food, medicine, and fruit, with their oil and other parts credited with many digestive, bodily, and eye benefits.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r9.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
ALUSI-FULL:v30p174/r9.claim: He says the Prophet praised olive wood as a blessed tooth-stick that freshens the mouth, and called it his own and the prophets' tooth-stick.

ELMALILI:95:1-3#3/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3#3/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:95:1-3#3/r3.claim: Mecca's security makes it holier in this respect than contested Holy Land sites and creates an ascent in the oaths from material taste toward spiritual security.

ELMALILI:95:1-3#3/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3#3/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:95:1-3#3/r6.claim: The familiar names Tīn, Zaytūn, Sinai, and the secure city evoke sacred places and their graded religious and worldly blessings, preparing for the answer about human creation.

ELMALILI:95:1-3/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r1.claim: Although tīn literally means fig, he prefers retaining Tīn and Zaytūn as proper names when they designate places, since translating a proper name by its lexical sense misidentifies its referent.

ELMALILI:95:1-3/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r10.speaker: ابن عباس، فخر الدين الرازي
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r10.claim: Al-Rāzī attributes to Ibn ʿAbbās two Holy Land mountains: the fig mountain is Jesus's mission site, and the olive mountain is Syria, where most Israelite prophets were sent.

ELMALILI:95:1-3/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r11.speaker: ابن زيد، كعب، ابن عباس
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r11.claim: Reported mosque identifications vary: Ibn Zayd says the Damascus and Jerusalem mosques; Kaʿb says Damascus and Iliya; one Ibn ʿAbbās report says Noah's mosque and Jerusalem.

ELMALILI:95:1-3/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r12.speaker: كعب، شهر بن حوشب
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r12.claim: Town identifications also vary: Kaʿb says Damascus and Jerusalem, while Shahr b. Hawshab says Kufa and Syria; Kufa means the land where Noah lived.

ELMALILI:95:1-3/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r13.claim: He favors the sacred-place resonance: the familiar fruits and their productive lands, mountains, towns, and mosques evoke beneficial provision, righteous effort, and places where prophetic religion began; together they point to the Holy Land and a secure city.

ELMALILI:95:1-3/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r2.speaker: حسن، مجاهد، عكرمة، إبراهيم النخعي، عطاء، مقاتل، كلبى، ابن عباس
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r2.claim: One reported view takes tīn and zaytūn literally as familiar fruits or their trees; the cited glosses call them the figs and olives people eat or press.

ELMALILI:95:1-3/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r3.claim: Without a contextual sign of metaphor, the evident meaning is the familiar fruits; their value as food, fruit, medicine, and trade may explain the oath.

ELMALILI:95:1-3/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r4.claim: Figs and olives may represent important provisions generally, while Sinai and the secure city represent places of spiritual provision; the oath can thus encompass material and spiritual sustenance.

ELMALILI:95:1-3/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r5.claim: The two fruits may also allude to female and male, as the oath in al-Layl suggests; on this view they can be translated literally.

ELMALILI:95:1-3/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r6.speaker: birçok müfessirîn، آلوسي
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r6.claim: Another view takes Tīn and Zaytūn as blessed places rather than fruit, supported by their pairing with Sinai and the secure city; al-Ālūsī favors this view.

ELMALILI:95:1-3/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r7.speaker: قتادة
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r7.claim: Qatāda, as transmitted by Ibn Jarīr, identifies Tīn as the mountain where Damascus stands and Zaytūn as the mountain where Jerusalem stands.

ELMALILI:95:1-3/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r8.speaker: عكرمة، ربيع
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r8.claim: ʿIkrima calls them two mountains; Rabīʿ locates them between Hamadan and Hulwan or among the mountains of Syria.

ELMALILI:95:1-3/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r9.speaker: أبو حبيب حارث بن محمر
ELMALILI:95:1-3/r9.claim: A report identifies them as Mount Tīnā and Mount Zaytā, named for the figs and olives that grow well there.

QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r1.claim: The surah’s central truth is that the human being’s sound innate nature aligns with faith and reaches its intended completion through it, while deviation makes the person fall low.

QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r10.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r10.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r10.claim: He cannot be certain of a specific interpretation, but considers places or memories connected to faith—or perhaps humanity’s original life in the Garden—the likeliest reading, fitting the surah’s central truth.

QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r2.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r2.claim: Mount Sinai is where Moses was called, and the secure city is Mecca and the Sacred House; both have clear ties to religion and faith.

QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r3.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r3.speaker: قول مأثور
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r3.claim: One reported view takes the fig as a reference to Mount Tina near Damascus.

QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r4.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r4.speaker: قول مأثور
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r4.claim: Another reported view connects the fig with the tree whose leaves Adam and his wife used to cover themselves in the Garden before descending to earthly life.

QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r5.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r5.speaker: قول مأثور
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r5.claim: A further reported view identifies the fig with the fig-growing mountain where Noah’s ark came to rest.

QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r6.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r6.speaker: قول مأثور
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r6.claim: Reported interpretations identify the olive with Mount Zayta in Jerusalem or Jerusalem itself.

QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r7.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r7.speaker: قول مأثور
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r7.claim: Another reported interpretation makes the olive the branch carried back by Noah’s dove, showing that the flood waters had receded and the earth had grown plants.

QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r8.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r8.speaker: قول مأثور
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r8.claim: Other views take the fig and olive literally as the familiar foods, or as symbols for the places where they grow.

QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r9.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r9.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:95:1/r9.claim: The Qur’an elsewhere mentions the olive tree near Sinai and olives with palms, but names the fig only here; these references do not settle the oath’s intended meaning.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r1.claim: The surah is called Wa-l-Tin in most tafsir books and codices, al-Tin in some sources including al-Tirmidhi's heading, and it is Meccan according to most scholars.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r2.speaker: ابن عطية
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r2.claim: Ibn Atiyya says he knows no disagreement among exegetes over its Meccan status; al-Qurtubi reports a Madinan view from Qatada and Ibn Abbas, but the sound report from Ibn Abbas says Meccan.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r3.claim: It is the twenty-eighth surah in revelation order, after al-Buruj and before al-Ilaf, and has eight verses.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r4.claim: The surah presents Islam as humanity's sound primordial nature and treats departures from its foundations as corruption and misguidance.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r5.claim: The oath's sacred places gesture toward four stages of divine law, suggesting Islam confirms those traditions and shares their foundations.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r8.claim: An emphatic opening oath marks the subject's importance, while its length builds anticipation for the sworn statement.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p419/r9.claim: The fig's form, dark peel, honeyed interior, pleasant taste, and easy cultivation display God's precise craft, knowledge, and power, and are a blessing to people.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p422/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p422/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p422/r1.claim: The oath at places associated with major revealed religions is a fine opening for the surah's claim that humanity was created in sound nature, able to recognize the Creator and His unity.

TABATABAI:95:3-6/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:95:3-6/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:95:3-6/r2.claim: Views on the fig and olive include the familiar fruits with their many benefits, the two trees, or the mountains near Damascus and Jerusalem; the mountains may take their names from those crops and be oaths for the regions where many prophets appeared. Other views also exist.

ASAD-NOTES:95:intro/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:95:intro/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:95:intro/r1.claim: The surah was revealed after surah 85, The Great Constellations.

ASAD-NOTES:95:intro/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:95:intro/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:95:intro/r2.claim: It states a fundamental moral truth shared by all true religious teachings.

ASAD-NOTES:95:intro/r3.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:95:intro/r3.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:95:intro/r3.claim: The surah's title keyword comes from the mention of the fig in its first verse.

CORPUSCORANICUM:95:1-3:kommentar/r3.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:95:1-3:kommentar/r3.speaker: Neuwirth
CORPUSCORANICUM:95:1-3:kommentar/r3.claim: Figs and olives are signs of God-given abundance, standing metonymically for creation and God's continuing provision for human livelihood.

CORPUSCORANICUM:95:1:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:95:1:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:95:1:anmerkung/r1.claim: Neuwirth proposes splitting the long, rhyming opening verse into two, by analogy with other oaths; the author objects that this would create two equally short verses with no Quranic parallel.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p370/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p370/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p370/r1.claim: The oath particle wa introduces an oath; Qur’anic oaths by objects and places bear witness to the premise stated after them.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p370/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p370/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p370/r2.claim: Al-Tīn means the Mount of Figs, a place known for producing figs, rather than the dried fruit; Farāhī explains the Arab place-naming custom.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r1.speaker: Nābighah Dhubyānī
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r1.claim: Farāhī cites a couplet in which al-Tīn is used as a place name, supporting the reading of the oath as a mountain.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r2.speaker: some people
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r2.claim: Some identify the mountain meant by al-Tīn as a mountain between Ḥalwān and Ḥamdān.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r3.speaker: Imām Farāhī
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r3.claim: Farāhī says al-Tīn is either Mount Jūdī or a nearby mountain, linking it with the post-Flood dispersal of humankind described in the Torah and placed near Jūdī by the Qur’an.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r4.claim: Al-Zaytūn likewise names the Mount of Olives, the site associated with Jesus’ preaching, worship, and supplication, rather than the olive or its tree.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r5.speaker: Imām Farāhī
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r5.claim: Farāhī says the Mount of Olives was named for its abundant olives and identifies it as the Gospel site where Jesus worshipped and prayed.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r6.speaker: Ibn ‘Abbās and Ka‘b
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r6.claim: Ibn ‘Abbās and Ka‘b interpret al-Zaytūn as Bayt al-Maqdis.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r7.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r7.speaker: Qatādah
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p371/r7.claim: Qatādah interprets al-Zaytūn as the mountain on which Bayt al-Maqdis is situated.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p374/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p374/r3.speaker: Imām Farāhī
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p374/r3.claim: Farāhī identifies the Mount of Figs with Jūdī and presents Adam’s and Noah’s episodes there as examples of divine retribution.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p374/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p374/r4.speaker: Imām Farāhī
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p374/r4.claim: Farāhī recounts that Adam and his wife forgot their covenant, ate the forbidden fruit after Satan’s temptation, and lost their success and heavenly clothing; the Qur’an recalls the episode.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p374/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p374/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p374/r5.claim: The account notes that the Torah identifies the leaves Adam and Eve used to cover themselves as fig leaves.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p374/r6.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p374/r6.speaker: Imām Farāhī
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p374/r6.claim: After Adam and Eve repented and God accepted them, He promised guidance and reward to its followers, making this a second covenant with Adam.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p375/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p375/r1.speaker: Imām Farāhī
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p375/r1.claim: The Adam episode has two sides: God removed one favor because of the broken promise, then gave another after Adam and Eve recognized their folly and repented.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p375/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p375/r2.speaker: Imām Farāhī
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p375/r2.claim: At Noah’s time God destroyed wrongdoers near the mountain and saved the righteous from the Flood, as shown in the Jūdī landing and Noah’s later promise of peace and blessings.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p375/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p375/r3.speaker: Imām Farāhī
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p375/r3.claim: Farāhī concludes that the Mount of Figs is a major site where God’s law of retribution became manifest.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p375/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p375/r4.speaker: Imām Farāhī
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p375/r4.claim: Farāhī says that in Jesus’ final years God transferred the sharī‘ah and trust from the Jews to Abraham’s other line; Jesus grieved for his people as they pursued his life.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p376/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p376/r1.speaker: Imām Farāhī
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p376/r1.claim: Farāhī cites Jesus’ rejected-stone saying and his warning that God’s kingdom would be taken from the Jews and given to a fruitful people as evidence of their lost trust.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p378/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p378/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p378/r1.claim: The oath sites testify to retribution and announce who merits God’s blessings and who faces His wrath.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p378/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p378/r2.speaker: Imām Farāhī
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p378/r2.claim: Farāhī orders the sites by historical and thematic resemblance: Adam precedes Jesus because of their likeness, then Sinai and Makkah evoke Moses and Muḥammad.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:95:1/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:95:1/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:95:1/r1.claim: God swears by four signs of His knowledge, artistry, and power—fig and olive as bodily food, Sinai as revelation's spiritual food, and secure Mecca—to affirm that He made humans best and endowed them to bear physical and spiritual duties (cf. 17:70).

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:95:1/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:95:1/r2.speaker: Müfessirler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:95:1/r2.claim: One symbolic view takes fig and olive as lands rich in those trees, Palestine and Syria, symbols of the blessing of prophetic teachings conveyed there.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:95:1/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:95:1/r3.speaker: Müfessirler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:95:1/r3.claim: Other symbolic interpretations identify the fig with Mecca's Sacred Mosque and the olive with Jerusalem's al-Aqsa Mosque.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:95:1/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:95:1/r4.speaker: Şevkânî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:95:1/r4.claim: Shawkani argues that these symbolic interpretations lack rational or transmitted evidence.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17#3/r11.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17#3/r11.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17#3/r11.claim: The ending returns to the opening: the one who sent the great revelations and their exalted laws is the wisest judge.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r1.claim: The opening oath may refer to the familiar fig and olive trees.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r10.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r10.speaker: مفسرون
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r10.claim: Another interpretation takes fig and olive as two Holy Land mountains, called Tour Tina and Tour Zaita in Syriac, where those trees grow.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r11.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r11.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r11.claim: On the mountain interpretation, the connection between the two names and what follows is not clear without strained reasoning.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r12.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r12.speaker: مفسرون
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r12.claim: A reported interpretation identifies three places of major prophetic missions: Jerusalem for Jesus, Sinai for Moses, and Mecca for Muhammad.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r13.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r13.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r13.claim: Al-Tibyān reads the oath as the three prophetic places and explains them as successive manifestations of Jesus, Moses, and Muhammad and their major religious communities.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r14.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r14.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r14.claim: Al-Tibyān says the oath ascends from the place of Jesus to Moses and then Muhammad, paralleling a Torah passage about Sinai, Seir, and Paran.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r15.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r15.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r15.claim: The author prefers the three prophetic locations because their relation to one another is clear on that reading.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r16.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r16.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r16.claim: The sequence begins with fig then olive, with olive ranked higher because God calls it blessed; it serves as fruit, food, and lamp oil.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r2.speaker: مفسرون
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r2.claim: Exegetes explain the paired trees as two kinds, one whose fruit has no seed and one whose fruit has a seed.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r20.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r20.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r20.claim: The oath progresses from fig to olive to Sinai to the secure city, moving from the noble to the noblest and ending at the home of the final, most honored mission.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r3.speaker: رسول الله
