SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r3.claim: A report says the Prophet received a plate of figs, ate them, and told his companions that if any fruit came from Paradise, it would be this one because Paradise's fruit has no seeds.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r4.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r4.claim: A report says Adam used fig leaves to cover his nakedness after it was exposed in Paradise.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r6.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r6.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r6.claim: The author speculates that the eight verses might correspond to Paradise's eight gates, but leans toward this being pure conjecture.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r7.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r7.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r7.claim: He notes numerical patterns elsewhere: eight repetitions of the blessing question in descriptions of Paradise and seven in warnings, corresponding to Paradise's and Hell's gates.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r8.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r8.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r8.claim: Other proposed numerical patterns say Sura al-Qadr has thirty words for Ramadan's days and places huwa at word 27 to signal the 27th night.

SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r9.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r9.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR:r17/r9.claim: The author cautions that many such numerical correspondences may simply be coincidences.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p420/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p420/r3.speaker: بعض المفسرين
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p420/r3.claim: Some exegetes identify the oath's fig and olive as the familiar trees, one fruit seedless and the other containing seeds.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p420/r4.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p420/r4.speaker: النبي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p420/r4.claim: A report says the Prophet ate a plate of figs and called it a fruit from Paradise because Paradise's fruit has no seeds; Adam also used fig leaves to cover himself.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p420/r5.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p420/r5.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p420/r5.claim: The olive is described as a blessed tree in the Qur'an.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p421/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p421/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p421/r1.claim: The author doubts that the fig's alleged Paradisal origin explains the surah's eight verses and eight gates of Paradise, calling that connection likely conjecture despite parallels elsewhere.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p421/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p421/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p421/r2.claim: He cites proposed numerical correspondences: eight Paradise descriptions, seven warnings for Hell, thirty words in al-Qadr, and its word “she” as the twenty-seventh word; he warns many such links may be coincidences.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p421/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p421/r3.speaker: بعض المفسرين
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p421/r3.claim: Another interpretation identifies the fig and olive with two Holy Land mountains, called Ṭūr Tīnā and Ṭūr Zaytā in Syriac, where those trees grow.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p422/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p422/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p422/r3.claim: The sequence begins with the fig and the more excellent olive, which God calls blessed; olive serves as fruit, food accompaniment, and lamp oil.

STUDYQURAN:95:1/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:95:1/r1.speaker: most commentators
STUDYQURAN:95:1/r1.claim: Most commentators take the fig and olive as earthly fruits, sworn by for their blessings and benefits.

STUDYQURAN:95:1/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:95:1/r2.speaker: others
STUDYQURAN:95:1/r2.claim: Some read them symbolically: fig as Damascus's mosque, perhaps Noah's mosque at Mount Jūdī, and olive as Jerusalem's Holy House; others identify the two mountains or cities.

STUDYQURAN:95:1/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:95:1/r3.speaker: others
STUDYQURAN:95:1/r3.claim: Another interpretation makes the fig the mosque of the Companions of the Cave and the olive the mosque in Jerusalem; another sees two Levantine mountains.

STUDYQURAN:95:1/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:95:1/r4.speaker: others
STUDYQURAN:95:1/r4.claim: A further view makes the fig the Garden leaves Adam and Eve used to cover themselves and the olive the blessed tree; these may foreshadow human abasement and intellect's light.

STUDYQURAN:95:intro/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:95:intro/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:95:intro/r1.claim: Al-Tīn is likely an early-middle Makkan sūrah revealed after Sūrah 85, though some consider it Madinan; it is named for the fig in verse 1.

STUDYQURAN:95:intro/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:95:intro/r3.speaker: the Prophet
STUDYQURAN:95:intro/r3.claim: A hadith says whoever recites the sūrah through its closing question and answers “Indeed” is among its witnesses.
